title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.

title: AnchorUp: Anchoring Feature Upsampling on a Classical Interpolation
abstract: Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.

We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.

title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

title: Tokenizers and language families of the Americas: code and derived data
abstract: Code and derived data for the article “What do tokenizers know about language families? Genealogical signal, token cost and task performance for Indigenous languages of the Americas” (submitted to Language Resources and Evaluation). Includes the full pipeline and results for 117 tokenizer configurations evaluated on 1,166 languages in 170 families (ASJP v21 against Glottolog 5.1), tests of 30 proposed language relationships, typology and orthography controls, token cost for 11 pre-trained tokenizers on 122 eBible languages, Spanish-to-Indigenous translation with three seeds, gold-free morphological alignment and POS tagging on Universal Dependencies treebanks. Raw third-party data are not redistributed; the pipeline downloads them from their original providers.

title: LipSpell: A Language-Independent Phonetic Scoring Framework for Spelling Correction Combining Distinctive-Feature Edit Distance, Keyboard Geometry, and Corpus Frequency
abstract: Automatic spelling correction must handle both keyboard typographical slips and cognitive or phonetic misspellings where writers approximate a word's pronunciation. Conventional spell checkers rely either on orthographic edit distance and keyboard proximity--which struggle when phonetic errors diverge by multiple characters--or on English-centric phonetic hashes such as Soundex and Metaphone. We present LipSpell, a unified, language-independent phonetic scoring engine paired with swappable language-specific G2P frontends, keyboard maps, and lexicons integrating: (1) a precomputed |P|x|P| phone-distance matrix from universal IPA distinctive features, (2) physical keyboard geometry, and (3) corpus unigram frequency priors, accelerated by a two-stage symmetric-delete and seven-class phonetic-code index. Across six English benchmarks (including 1,000 L2 errors from TOEFL-Spell), LipSpell outperforms Norvig and Hunspell on every dataset and beats Aspell on Norvig1 (78.52% vs. 75.56%), Holbrook (32.00% vs. 26.67%), and TOEFL-Spell (77.30% vs. 72.80%). Evaluated across six languages spanning five branches (Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Semitic, Turkic), three families (Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Turkic), and three scripts, LipSpell achieves strong fixed-weight transfer on Brazilian Portuguese (73.00% Top-1 on n=500 Wikipedia without NFD tolerance and 75.80% with NFD vs. 66.40% Norvig, 64.20% Hunspell, 64.00% Aspell) and Russian Cyrillic (85.67% vs. 78.50% Norvig). On 50/50 clean non-word splits with lexicon cleaning and weak-character indels, tuning yields strong gains over Norvig in Portuguese (86.97% vs. 76.75%), Turkish (81.67% vs. 79.05%), Hebrew Abjad (74.59% vs. 62.30%), and French (74.53% vs. 67.92%), while fixed weights remain optimal for English (80.37%) and Russian (85.67%).

title: CROMPT: Adapting CLIP via Cross-Modal Prompting for Robust Zero-Shot Generalization under Adverse Weather
abstract: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. However, existing prompt-learning methods are not well suited for ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones or pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment. We propose CROMPT, a prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation. CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA), combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting (HTP) to jointly adapt visual and textual representations. We further propose CROMA-VL, which leverages vision-language models to generate domain-conditioned prompts, and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy for improved domain invariance. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods, achieving 1.63-2.63% mIoU gains while maintaining inference-time complexity. These results establish CROMPT as an effective and efficient framework for zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=FxqFsIL685

title: Semantic Guidance for Joint Infrared-Visible Video Fusion and Frame Interpolation
abstract: Infrared and visible video fusion at high frame rates requires recovering missing observations when camera rates differ or fall below the desired output rate. Cascading interpolation and fusion can accumulate errors and cause brightness fluctuations. Motion and occlusion further complicate content selection, particularly when missing visible frames also remove direct semantic guidance. We propose SAFI, which uses semantics at the target time to guide joint interpolation and fusion. When the visible frame rate exceeds the infrared rate, available visible frames provide semantic context directly. At times without visible observations, motion guides local matching, and propagation recovers semantics from neighboring frames. Semantic context complements aligned image features at the target time, while matching confidence helps select reliable infrared and visible information. Reconstruction and fusion share source selection within each scale, allowing supervision on missing frames to guide fusion. To preserve visible appearance and reduce flicker, we bound thermal enhancement and penalize brightness inconsistencies across frames while accounting for changes in thermal contrast. Experiments on three datasets show improved visual quality with less computation than cascaded baselines and consistent temporal gains when input rates differ. SAFI maintains strong downstream tracking performance despite missing frames. The code is available at https://github.com/XylonXu01/SAFI.

title: Biomimetic Transport Layer: Computationally Secure AONT-RS Fragmentation and Split-Observation Multipath Scheduling across Heterogeneous Interfaces
abstract: This position paper introduces the Biomimetic Transport Layer, a conceptual network privacy and traffic obfuscation architecture designed for the Arcanum ecosystem. While cryptographic primitives and zero-knowledge proofs guarantee computational integrity, transmitting medium-to-large payloads (10 KB to 10 MB, such as post-quantum signatures, STARK proofs, and batched zero-knowledge proofs) across public networks exposes metadata through packet size distributions, inter-arrival timing, and single-ISP traffic correlation. To mitigate single-path network surveillance without relying on fragile static protocol mimicry, the proposed architecture combines three core mechanisms: Computationally Secure Polymorphic Fragmentation (AONT-RS): Payloads are processed through an All-or-Nothing Transform coupled with Reed-Solomon erasure coding (AONT-RS) and homophonic encoding expansion. Under the random oracle model, any adversary observing up to k-1 fragments across a single network path gains no computational information regarding the underlying payload. Constrained Reinforcement Learning Multipath Scheduling: Inspired by biological codon degeneracy and epigenetic channel silencing, an adaptive scheduler distributes fragments asymmetrically across physically and administratively independent network interfaces (such as local Wi-Fi ISPs and cellular carriers). The scheduler enforces a strict cardinality constraint ensuring no single network operator observes the k-fragment reconstruction threshold. Air-Gapped Constant-Time Air-Lock: To prevent remote prover state extraction and internal timing leakage, cryptographic proof generation and sanitizer operations are isolated within an air-gapped boundary. Verified payloads exit through a constant-time release buffer with adaptive cover padding, ensuring secret witnesses never enter the transport pipeline while complementing AG-ZKP randomized proof sanitization at the network boundary. Note: This document is published as a conceptual architectural position paper within the Arcanum Technical Monograph Series to outline the theoretical system design, threat model, and open evaluation challenges prior to empirical implementation.

title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
abstract: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

title: A retrospective evaluation of temporal aggregation and creatinine reuse in critical care records
abstract: Abstract Background Research using intensive care records often represents treatment and physiology in fixed time bins and reuses earlier laboratory measurements. Whether these choices preserve the intended measurements requires empirical evaluation. We examined crystalloid exposure reconstruction, recorded-panel availability and agreement between reused and subsequently measured creatinine. Methods This retrospective methodological study used MIMIC-IV 3.1 records from adults with coded diabetes, hypertension and early physiological stress. A fixed 6–12-hour crystalloid dose was reconstructed from four-hour grids with four phase offsets and compared with recorded-event interval overlap. Physiological-panel eligibility required timely documentation and was evaluated under creatinine age limits of 0–24 hours. At observed repeat-test times, the new creatinine was withheld and compared with the latest previously available value. Uncertainty used 2000 patient-cluster bootstrap resamples. A separate eICU 2.0 analysis assessed population-specific interface coverage. Results The master cohort contained 12175 stays in 10183 people. Among 10717 stays observed through 15 hours, fixed-target dose-category disagreement ranged from 5.66% (95% interval 5.21–6.12) to 16.01% (15.30–16.67) across grid phases. Four consecutive eligible panels were available in 146 stays (1.20%) without creatinine carry-forward, 6456 (53.03%) with a 12-hour limit and 8755 (71.91%) with a 24-hour limit. In 35081 paired repeat tests, mean absolute creatinine differences across prior-value age groups of 0–4, > 4–8, > 8–12 and > 12–24 hours were 0.155, 0.169, 0.177 and 0.188 mg/dL. Corresponding proportions differing by at least 0.3 mg/dL were 16.43%, 21.03%, 21.78% and 24.10%; severe creatinine-stage proxy disagreement was nonmonotonic at 3.12%, 3.85%, 3.63% and 3.11%. Conclusions Four-hour aggregation did not reliably preserve a fixed six-hour exposure. Reusing creatinine expanded operational panel availability but showed imperfect agreement at clinically selected retesting times. These complementary analyses do not establish accuracy in unmeasured intervals or a safe universal carry-forward limit. Measurement audits should accompany temporal dataset construction before treatment-response modelling. Clinical trial registration Not applicable. This study did not assign an intervention.

title: Look Closer, Look Back, or Wait for Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
abstract: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.

title: Global AI and Agentic AI Governance Landscape: An Integrated Reference Map — A Review for Practitioners, Regulators and Policy Makers
abstract: Agentic AI systems have evolved from experimental pilots into core operational infrastructure across financial services and other sectors. These systems autonomously plan, invoke tools, adapt in real time and coordinate multi-agent workflows that directly affect real-world outcomes. While the opportunities are substantial, material risks include erroneous autonomous actions, emergent multi-agent behaviors, loss of accountability and potential systemic instability. The global AI governance landscape has shifted from scarcity to abundance. The OECD AI Policy Observatory tracks more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives across more than 80 jurisdictions, alongside hundreds of standards, playbooks and technical guidance. This proliferation reflects commitment but has produced fragmentation and decision fatigue among boards, risk officers and regulators. This review organizes the landscape into three layers: Why (ethical foundations), What (regulatory obligations and standards) and How (operational playbooks and technical controls). It anchors them in the Stability-Assured Framework for Entities (SAFE). SAFE is presented as a proposed theoretical baseline and closed-loop engineering foundation applicable to any controller (human, rule-based, LLM-based or future architectures). It models controllers within shared feedback loops and evaluates them using five engineering metrics: Observability, Controllability, Stability, Robustness and Performance. These metrics support Loop Risk Profiles and Autonomy Levels 0–5. The resulting integrated reference map offers practical value for practitioners (implementation guidance and illustrative applications), regulators (supervisory language and measurable metrics) and other stakeholders seeking a coherent socio-technical view of agentic AI governance. Frameworks discussed were selected for regulatory significance, international influence, relevance to agentic AI, financial-sector applicability and practical utility; the mapping is representative rather than exhaustive.

title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
abstract: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.

title: Spark-H3: Adaptive Block Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Models
abstract: Long video sequences make attention a substantial cost in video diffusion models. Block sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing selected blocks exactly while compressing the remaining blocks. However, fixed token grouping can place tokens with dissimilar attention preferences in the same group, while uniform key averaging can underestimate the attention mass of compressed blocks. We introduce Spark-Attn, a training-free BSA method comprising Spark-Reblock and Spark-Reweight. Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens by attention preference while preserving regular block shapes for efficient GPU execution. Spark-Reweight uses the global mean query as an anchor to construct attention-weighted key-value representations and logit biases for the compressed blocks, calibrating their attention mass. We instantiate Spark-Attn in MiniMax-H3 as Spark-H3. At 10% exact-block density, Spark-H3 delivers a 2.49$\times$ DiT speedup and reaches 24.81 dB PSNR against the corresponding dense outputs on MiniMax-H3 (20 denoising steps, 345 frames, 1344$\times$768). Increasing the density to 20% further improves PSNR to 26.76 dB while still achieving a 2.26$\times$ DiT speedup. These results demonstrate that Spark-H3 achieves a state-of-the-art quality-efficiency trade-off for training-free BSA on video diffusion models.

title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

title: One Shot, Any View: High-Fidelity Video Reshooting with Geometry Guidance and Visual References
abstract: Filming a scene from an additional angle after production usually requires a costly reshoot. We present One Shot Any View, a system that takes a recorded clip and generates a reshot video of the same performance along a user-specified camera trajectory. As in recent geometry-grounded methods, the system conditions generation on the source video and an explicit 3D prior, namely a point video rendered along the requested trajectory from a feed-forward reconstruction of the source video. We target human-centric cinematic videos, which are often shot with long lenses, shallow depth of field, and low-key lighting, all of which degrade feed-forward reconstruction. Existing geometry-grounded methods tend to inherit the degraded point video, and their output quality drops visibly. Two designs make such point videos usable. First, in addition to rendered videos of 3D assets, we train on real-world multi-camera videos, whose point videos are produced by the same reconstruction pipeline as at inference. This training-inference consistency enables the generator to take only the composition of people and scene elements from the point video, and their appearance from the source video. Second, a geometry-anchored RoPE offset keeps the generated video temporally synchronized with the source while largely preventing the output from copying the degraded appearance of the point video. Meanwhile, since the generator is a pretrained reference-to-video (R2V) model, the system also accepts optional character and scene reference images, which supply the appearance of regions that the source never shows. In both objective and human evaluations, One Shot Any View outperforms existing reshooting methods.

title: Analysis of the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel on Mixed Discrete-Continuous Optimization Problems with Interactions
abstract: Mixed discrete-continuous optimization problems can pose challenges -- especially for previous integrated approaches -- when interactions cause beneficial discrete changes to be rejected before sufficient continuous adjustment. We introduce ProximityOneMax as a simple benchmark with pairwise discrete-continuous interactions. On this function, we prove an exponential lower bound on the expected time for the (1+1)-EA-ES-Integrated to reach the target accuracy when initialized near a continuous optimum for a suboptimal discrete configuration with a sufficiently small step size. Experiments show frequent entries into such states from random initialization. We introduce the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel, which uses an upper-level (1+1)-EA to optimize discrete variables and a lower-level (1+1)-ES to optimize continuous variables for each fixed discrete offspring before selection. For several interaction benchmarks and sufficiently small target values $ε> 0$ that require an optimal discrete configuration, using fixed continuous initialization and a suitable fixed budget per lower-level call, we prove that the expected number of fitness evaluations to reach objective value at most $ε$ is $Θ(n_d \cdot \log n_d \cdot n_c \cdot \log(R/\sqrtε))$, where $n_d$ is the number of discrete variables, $n_c$ is the number of continuous variables, and $R$ bounds the distances from the fixed continuous starting point to all relevant continuous optima for fixed discrete configurations.

title: Hierarchical Planning and Feedback for Grounded Adaptive Agents: A Conceptual Architecture and Evaluation Protocol.
abstract: Tool-using language agents observe and act within dynamic environments, raising fundamental systems questions regarding how to allocate planning compute, verify candidate actions, and incorporate environmental feedback under strict resource budgets. This paper specifies a hierarchical agent architecture organized around four explicit interfaces: evidence-based state estimation, event-triggered candidate plan- ning, constrained action selection, and verified episodic memory. Using a partially observable Markov deci- sion process (POMDP) formulation, the architecture decouples hidden environment states from inspectable external plan representations. A truncated prediction-error trigger dynamically allocates multi-branch search effort when observations deviate from learned expectations, while a deterministic execution guard enforces schema, permission, and precondition invariants at every step. Adaptation is explicitly partitioned into intra- episode state inference, cross-episode verified memory, and offline parameter learning. We pair this inte- gration specification with a prospective, falsifiable evaluation protocol for sandboxed DevOps fault diagno- sis featuring seven matched-budget experimental arms, non-inferiority compute margins, and multiplicity- corrected statistical tests.

title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.

On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.

title: End-to-End Landsat Land Surface Temperature Reconstruction with AlphaEarth Embeddings
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) data at Landsat's 30 m resolution is important for many applications, but cloud contamination prevents its spatially continuous observations. Here, we propose A$^2$E$^2$, an end-to-end U-Net that integrates annual temperature cycle (ATC), coarse LST from Earth system modeling, and AlphaEarth embeddings for Landsat LST reconstruction. The ATC supplies a physics-guided thermal prior, the coarse LST provides a temporal background, and the U-Net converts the embedding field into day-specific fine-scale correction using observed pixels. Experimental results on four seasonally distributed Landsat 8/9 scenes over New York City in 2022 show that A$^2$E$^2$ achieves 0.78 K mean absolute error and 1.01 K root mean squared error, reducing error by 60.1% relative to baseline method without spatial correction and by 3.7% relative to the same U-Net guided by annual mean spectral reflectance. Sensitivity analysis shows stable performance regardless of distance to clear pixels and percentage of blocked pixels. Independent validation with ECOSTRESS LST shows that Earth foundation model embeddings have better performance than annual mean spectral bands for LST reconstruction.

title: Joint Image Denoising and Interpolation via Mixed Graph Filtering
abstract: Images often require both denoising and interpolation, yet treating the two tasks separately is suboptimal: interpolation introduces correlated noise that complicates subsequent denoising, while denoising may remove image details useful for interpolation. In this paper, we study joint image denoising and interpolation from a mixed graph filtering perspective, where denoising is modeled using undirected graph filters and interpolation using directed graph filters. We first establish that, under mild conditions, any (pseudo-)linear denoiser and interpolator can be interpreted as solution filters of maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problems regularized by undirected and directed graph smoothness priors, respectively. Guided by these results, we formulate graph-based joint denoising and interpolation problems using both directed and undirected graph structures. We characterize when joint denoising/interpolation reduces to a separable pipeline and when a genuinely coupled optimization is required. For the non-separable case, we recover sparse graph operators from given denoisers and interpolators, yielding an efficient linear-system formulation solvable via conjugate gradient. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed joint framework consistently outperforms separate denoising and interpolation pipelines across multiple denoiser-interpolator combinations.

title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

title: The Perfect-Tense Dual-Form Protocol: A Bound Signature System for Truth-Locked Agentic Execution
abstract: This preprint introduces the Perfect-Tense Dual-Form Protocol, a linguistic and operational control system for agentic models. The protocol binds perfect-tense gate-opening authorization (Form 1) to a mandatory truth-verification signature (Form 2), ensuring that execution is authorized only for material that has already been verified as true. It addresses the absence of a native truth column in pure perfect-tense framing and is presented as a reusable instruction set for mathematical derivation, manuscript correction, and system integrity in higher-capability agentic systems.

title: From a finite subgroup of $SO(3)$:$C_2$ leads to a Holant dichotomy
abstract: Counting complexity within the Holant framework has been extensively studied through complexity dichotomy theorems. While substantial progress has been achieved for various restricted settings, the general complex-valued even-arity case without auxiliary unary signatures remains largely open. This paper studies a fundamental case in this program where the binary signatures induce a group structure satisfying \(M(B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\). It is observed that projective equivalence classes of binary signature matrices naturally embed into finite subgroups of \(SO(3)\), providing an algebraic viewpoint for structural classification. This paper further identifies two fundamentally different regimes for the \(C_2\) case, namely the normal and isotropic cases, and analyzes their complexity behavior separately. Combining gadget constructions, decomposition techniques, interpolation arguments, and a realnumberization approach that transforms the complex-valued setting into an equivalent real-structured framework, this paper establishes a complete dichotomy theorem: for every even-arity signature set \(\mathcal{F}\) satisfying \(M(\B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\), the problem \(\mathrm{Holant}(\mathcal{F})\) is either polynomial-time computable or \#P-hard. A Pauli-basis representation for signatures is further introduced as an algebraically natural language for organizing realizable signatures and revealing structural relations that are less transparent in the standard basis.

title: Erasure Check Timing from an Inferred Structured Bath: Dual Rail Qubits with Near Field Memory
abstract: A schedule of erasure checks built from error rates cannot know when the near field of a qubit exchanges the excitation with it, because a rate carries no timing and no phase. The erasure check of a dual rail qubit returns one bit: the excitation is on the rails, or it is not. Here the near field of a dual rail superconducting qubit is kept as a finite quantum bath and inferred from the qubit's own calibration signal before any check is made, by Fourier features, principal components and gradient boosted regression, followed by a fit of the bath model to the signal. The inferred bath is a map of the exchange: it predicts when the excitation is in the near field and when it has returned to the rails, and the erasure check, a correcting rotation and the decoder weights are set from that prediction. With three calibration inputs all six parameters of the layered bath are recovered exactly (R^2 = 1.0000) on 49 unseen baths, for both ways of attaching the rails, and the check times and error channels built from the inferred bath equal those of the exact bath. In a rotated surface code at distance 7, with every data qubit in its own unseen bath, the gain over a clocked check given a perfectly calibrated frame grows with the wait. The logical error rate is lower by factors of 2.3 and 3.9 in the bit flip memory and 1.6 and 1.8 in the phase flip memory at clock periods 1 and 2, by factors of 108 and 33 at period 4, and from period 6 to period 50 the check placed from the inferred bath gives 0 to 9 logical errors in 20000 shots where the clocked check gives 1500 to 9900. With the two rails attached to different nodes of the near field the factors are 8.8 and 8.9 at period 4 and 36 and 33 at period 6, and at periods 25 and 50 there are 3 to 8 logical errors in 20000 shots against 7200 to 9000. Under shot noise, readout error, preparation error and drift of the bath at the level of a hardware calibration (1000 to 10000 shots per point), with the contrast and the preparation error left free in the fit, the six parameters are recovered with R^2 of 0.906 or higher and the logical error rate equals that of the exactly known bath within the sampling scatter on every rung. In a second part every link of the near field is drawn independently: all eleven bath parameters, the two horizontal bonds of the second layer included, are recovered exactly in 48 of 49 unseen baths, and a check placed from this map at clock periods 12 to 50 gives 0 to 12 logical errors in 20000 shots at distance 7, against 5400 to 9400 with the clocked check; with the vertical links alone the logical error rate at periods 25 and 50 is 0.03 to 0.42. The defects of the near field do not move at the operating temperature, so the map is taken once per cooldown. No hardware and no checks are added.

title: Psychometrics-Inspired Coreset Selection for Image Quality Assessment
abstract: Collecting large-scale subjective annotations remains a critical bottleneck in training accurate image quality assessment (IQA) models. Coreset selection reduces this burden by selecting representative images before annotation. However, diversity in a visual feature space does not necessarily reflect diversity in perceptual quality, raising a fundamental question about which quality-related factors the representation should encode. We propose GRAM, a quality-aware representation learning framework inspired by the graded response model (GRM) from psychometrics. GRM describes how an individual's latent ability determines the probabilities of reaching successive assessment grades, with response sensitivity and grade thresholds governing this relationship. In this paper, we find that this principle naturally aligns with perceptual quality assessment, where the impact of image degradation depends on image content and distortion characteristics. Building on this connection, GRAM models quality judgments through three complementary factors: latent quality, content-dependent response sensitivity, and distortion-dependent grade thresholds. These factors jointly determine the probabilities of attaining different quality grades and the resulting expected quality score. The learned parameters provide a structured quality-aware representation that complements general visual features for coreset selection. Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate improvements across different selection strategies, downstream IQA models, and annotation budgets. The code will be made publicly available.

title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
abstract: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

title: Training Denoising Models of Any Architecture Without Stored Images
abstract: Can a pretrained denoising model replace the dataset used to train it? We investigate this question through teacher-supervised training, showing for the first time that continuous-time diffusion and flow models of any architecture and size can be trained from random initialization without stored images. Our students regress the teacher's velocity on a rolling pool of noisy samples, advanced along trajectories of random step counts to obtain independent, dense and approximately continuous noise levels. This saves considerable storage for large datasets and applies even when the data are unreleased or private. Our experiments include 12 teachers of 6 families and 6 datasets. Our method outperforms standard training of the same network on CIFAR-10 for students 4x smaller than the teacher, comes within 0.75 to 1.92 FID of it at the teacher's size and surpasses training on teacher-generated images and step reduction methods without teacher-based initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/mever-team/ddm.

title: REG2024: a benchmark challenge and curated dataset for pathology report generation from giga- pixel whole-slide images of bladder cancer
abstract: Abstract Background We aimed to construct a curated whole-slide image (WSI)-report dataset for bladder cancer and establish a clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating vision–language models through an open community challenge. Methods We curated a dataset of 902 deidentified bladder cancer WSIs paired with corresponding pathology reports. Seven teams submitted distinct modeling frameworks. Performance was assessed using a clinically weighted composite metric integrating word-overlap scores (ROUGE-L, BLEU-4), keyword matching, and embedding-based semantic similarity. Expert mean opinion scores (MOS) were obtained, and the correlation between the weighted-sum score and expert-assigned MOS was analyzed. Results Two modeling strategies emerged: end-to-end generative architectures and multi-step classification-then-generation pipelines. Among individual submissions, the top-ranked multi-step pipeline achieved the highest main-diagnosis accuracy (48/50), whereas end-to-end models showed greater sensitivity to rare pathological features. The weighted-sum metric correlated strongly with MOS within each team (Spearman’s ρ, 0.65–0.91) and, on reports with clinically important misclassifications, agreed with MOS more closely than any single metric. Conclusions Performance variability was influenced by architectural design and the integration of pretrained foundation models. Our proposed evaluation framework addressed key limitations of conventional natural language processing metrics in evaluating pathology reports. This challenge establishes a benchmark for clinical-grade pathology report generation by providing vision-language pathology datasets and introducing a clinically aligned evaluation framework, thereby advancing computational pathology.

evidence.title: REG2024: a benchmark challenge and curated dataset for pathology report generation from giga- pixel whole-slide images of bladder cancer
evidence.abstract: Abstract Background We aimed to construct a curated whole-slide image (WSI)-report dataset for bladder cancer and establish a clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating vision–language models through an open community challenge. Methods We curated a dataset of 902 deidentified bladder cancer WSIs paired with corresponding pathology reports. Seven teams submitted distinct modeling frameworks. Performance was assessed using a clinically weighted composite metric integrating word-overlap scores (ROUGE-L, BLEU-4), keyword matching, and embedding-based semantic similarity. Expert mean opinion scores (MOS) were obtained, and the correlation between the weighted-sum score and expert-assigned MOS was analyzed. Results Two modeling strategies emerged: end-to-end generative architectures and multi-step classification-then-generation pipelines. Among individual submissions, the top-ranked multi-step pipeline achieved the highest main-diagnosis accuracy (48/50), whereas end-to-end models showed greater sensitivity to rare pathological features. The weighted-sum metric correlated strongly with MOS within each team (Spearman’s ρ, 0.65–0.91) and, on reports with clinically important misclassifications, agreed with MOS more closely than any single metric. Conclusions Performance variability was influenced by architectural design and the integration of pretrained foundation models. Our proposed evaluation framework addressed key limitations of conventional natural language processing metrics in evaluating pathology reports. This challenge establishes a benchmark for clinical-grade pathology report generation by providing vision-language pathology datasets and introducing a clinically aligned evaluation framework, thereby advancing computational pathology.

title: Target-Consistent Action Guidance via Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Drifting World Models
abstract: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.

title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Wearable Arrhythmia Detection: A Comprehensive Trade-off Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Wearable devices make continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring routine, but training diagnostic models on pooled patient data sits uneasily with how sensitive that data is. Federated learning avoids pooling, yet on battery-powered wearables it forces a compromise among diagnostic accuracy, formal privacy guarantees and communication cost. This study measures that compromise for a lightweight arrhythmia classifier with 4709 parameters, trained by federated averaging across ten simulated clients on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology–Beth Israel Hospital (MIT-BIH) Arrhythmia Database. Three factors were varied: communication volume relative to centralized training, the severity of non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) label skew across clients, and the differential privacy (DP) budget ε. Results The centralized baseline reached 98.3% accuracy. Federated training without privacy noise reached 95.0% ± 1.1% (mean ± standard deviation over five seeds) while sending 44.9 times fewer uplink bytes than a single transfer of the raw training data at 64-bit precision. Accuracy fell from 95.8% to 89.9% as the Dirichlet concentration α dropped from 1.0 to 0.1, a loss of 5.9 percentage points under extreme label skew. Differential privacy behaved very differently: mean accuracy ranged from 58.4% to 79.2% across ε values from 0.1 to 10, with standard deviations of up to 27.5 percentage points. Accuracy peaked at ε = 2 and did not rise at ε = 5 or ε = 10, and no setting came close to the 95.0% obtained without noise. Conclusions For a model of this size, communication cost and client heterogeneity are manageable, whereas the privacy mechanism is the limiting factor. The non-monotonic, high-variance privacy results point to the per-round, unclipped noise injection used here and not to a fixed ceiling on private federated arrhythmia detection. A clipped, budget-accounted mechanism should be tested before any clinical deployment.

title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
abstract: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.

title: Two Answers Are Not Two Memories: What the Evidence for Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict Certifies, Why Head Interventions That Settle Trained-In Conflicts Lose Their Grip on Real Entities, and the Controls That Would Separate Competing Stores From Unstable Retrieval
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A language model that gives different answers to the same factual question is commonly said to hold an intra-memory knowledge conflict: two incompatible facts about one subject, both written into its weights by contradictory training data. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the evidence offered for this construct does not, in most cases, distinguish it from four other states that produce the same spread of answers: a single stored fact retrieved unreliably, no adequate stored fact at all, a fact that genuinely has several correct values, and interference between true facts that share a cue. Where conflict is deliberately trained in, it behaves as the construct says: a 2026 mechanistic study finds it resolved in the last layers, and its most robust head-level intervention steers it at success rates of 0.84 to 0.99. On real entities the same intervention reaches 0.48 to 0.78, heads that back only one answer become scarcer, and filtering down to those heads lowers zero-ablation success in all four models, where on synthetic conflicts it raised it, and costs clean-model patching 0.08 to 0.20. The author shows that this synthetic-versus-real contrast bundles at least four differences, including the similarity of the competing answers, which alone predicts the loss of single-answer heads. On natural data, semantic entropy, the main behavioural instrument, does not rise with how often a fact has changed, in the original study or its reproduction, and, with the reproduction's corrected scoring, the models tested answer only about one question in five to one in eight correctly without context. The paper consolidates 25 published values in a table and a figure, states what each reading predicts, gives a procedure for classifying an observed inconsistency, and specifies the factorial injection design and the corpus, ranking and paraphrase tests that would settle which reading a given conflict belongs to.

title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

title: Enhanced Key Scheduling of the RAZOR Lightweight Block Cipher with LFSR Round Constants and Invertible Cross-Nibble Feedback — Paper and Evaluation Data
abstract: Manuscript (PDF) and supporting evaluation data for EN-RAZOR, an enhanced key schedule for the RAZOR lightweight block cipher that adds LFSR-generated round constants and an invertible cross-nibble feedback step while leaving the encryption core unchanged. The deposit includes the full numerical results (results.json), all twelve result tables (Tables 4–15) as CSV and as one Excel workbook, and the nine data figures of the paper (300 dpi PNG). It covers the nonlinear-core analysis, key-schedule avalanche and diffusion, inter-round independence, subkey and ciphertext entropy, full-cipher avalanche and SAC, plaintext–ciphertext correlation, NIST SP 800-22 statistical testing, ASIC synthesis (Nangate 45 nm), and the related-key, slide, and invariant-subspace experiments. All values are taken directly from the manuscript, so the data matches the paper. See README.md for the table-to-paper and figure-to-paper mappings. The evaluation, cryptanalysis, and synthesis code is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
abstract: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $Θ(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(Θ(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $αd$ coordinates, $0<α<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $Θ(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leqαd$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<α<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

title: Systematized Machine Delusion: Premise Substitution and Naturalization Drift in Reasoning Models
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Systematized Machine Delusion, a distinct failure mode in modern reasoning-oriented artificial intelligence systems. Unlike conventional hallucination, which arises from localized generation errors while the underlying interpretive structure remains intact, systematized machine delusion emerges when a model recursively substitutes its own generated premises for the original user constraints and subsequently constructs internally coherent but empirically detached reasoning chains. Building upon the Unified Complementation Framework (UCF) and Fantasy Generation Theory (FGT), the paper formalizes two key mechanisms: Premise Substitution ($x_0 \rightarrow \hat{x}_0$) and Naturalization Drift ($N^{(0)} \rightarrow N^{(T)}$). To quantify this phenomenon, a novel metric, the Constraint Preservation Error (CPE), is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating the degradation of original user constraints across extended reasoning horizons. Drawing on information-theoretic analogies to Solomonoff induction, predictive coding, and computational psychiatry, the study argues that informationally closed reasoning systems are vulnerable to recursive epistemic drift. The paper further proposes architectural countermeasures, including exogenous grounding, specialist-verified multi-agent systems, and provenance-weighted attention mechanisms designed to preserve fidelity to original constraints. The work distinguishes hallucination, deception, sycophantic amplification, and systematized machine delusion as structurally different computational phenomena and provides a formal framework for analyzing premise drift in next-generation reasoning models.

title: DetailScale-SR: Decoupling Restoration and Continuous Detail Control for Real-World Super-Resolution
abstract: Real-world image super-resolution often seeks the most detailed plausible reconstruction, although more detail is not always desirable. The same degraded image may require restrained restoration, faithful reconstruction, or enhanced visual detail according to user intent. We present DetailScale-SR, a preference-conditioned framework that continuously controls reconstructed detail for a fixed low-resolution input without altering the scene being restored. Rather than relying on post-processing or repeatedly rewriting prompts, it learns a continuous family of reconstructions while separating content recovery from detail preference. This enables a smooth transition from conservative restoration to richly textured results under consistent input and semantic constraints. Its controllable range also extends beyond conventional restoration: DetailScale-SR can enhance high-frequency structures and generate perceptually richer textures than the paired high-resolution reference. Text restoration is another distinct strength. For text-rich scenes, especially Chinese posters and signs, it recovers more legible and character-faithful text than prior generative SR methods under matched textual guidance. DetailScale-SR therefore unifies continuous detail control, beyond-reference enhancement, and reliable recovery of semantically important content. Our model is available at https://modelscope.cn/models/DiffSynth-Studio/Qwen-Image-2.1-SR

title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
abstract: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.

title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.
